metadata.title: Why a Glowing PET Scan Doesn't Actually Show Cancer
metadata.purpose: vox-explainer slate cut of Cancer Nanomedicine card 13. Source chapter: cancer-nanomedicine/chapters/06-nano-enabled-imaging-and-contrast.md (the FDG-PET proxy mechanism only).
metadata.color_semantics: TEAL #1F6F5C = true signal / correct finding / the proxy that holds; CRIMSON #BF3339 = the wrong interpretation / false positive / the gap between proxy and biology; GOLD = editor's-pen highlight once only; never swap mid-film

style_bible.color_palette: cream ground, charcoal serif type, teal = correct / true, crimson = broken / false, gold highlighter as single editor's-pen voice

metadata.note: Card exclusions honored: NO five-modality tour (MRI/CT/fluorescence/photoacoustic), NO biodistribution decision tree, NO activatable probes, NO anatomical/molecular hierarchy section. Keep: signal = metabolism proxy, so false positives (inflammation, brown fat, healing wounds) and false negatives (low-glycolytic tumors) happen. Illustrative example: 58-year-old patient, 3 reactive lymph nodes after breast cancer surgery, all three with high FDG uptake from upper-respiratory infection — no malignant cells found on biopsy.

beats.narration_text: Three lymph nodes lighting up on PET. A surgical team moves to plan salvage radiation. The scan is technically correct. The diagnosis is completely wrong.

card.copy: Why a Glowing PET Scan Doesn't Actually Show Cancer
card.sub: the signal is real — the cause is wrong

beats.narration_text: FDG-PET is the standard tool for staging cancer and checking for recurrence. Bright spots indicate tracer accumulation. Surgeons and oncologists act on those spots every day.
beats.scene_description: a printed PET scan coronal image pinned to newsprint ground — warm amber-bright lymph node uptake regions visible against dark background, editorial desaturated treatment; slow push-in toward the bright nodes
beats.image_prompt: B02, a printed FDG-PET scan coronal image pinned like a clipping to aged newsprint, warm amber-colored hotspots of radiotracer uptake visible in the chest and neck region against dark background, desaturated editorial reproduction, flat print, three glowing nodes clearly visible

beats.narration_text: PET is used to detect cancer. The tracer does not target cancer cells. What is it actually measuring — and when does that distinction cause the wrong clinical decision?

card.copy: A PET scan is used to detect cancer. The tracer isn't looking for cancer cells. What is it actually measuring — and when does that difference matter?

beats.new_visual_element: [CARD] THE QUESTION on screen — gap formula

beats.narration_text: FDG is fluorodeoxyglucose — a radioactive glucose analog. Cells take it up through the same transporters they use for sugar and trap it inside. The camera counts where the decay occurs.

lines: into the cell through a sugar door
the isotope decays — the scanner sees

beats.new_visual_element: [GRAPHIC] FDG uptake — glucose enters, gets trapped

beats.narration_text: PET does not see cancer. It measures glucose metabolism — specifically hexokinase activity and glucose-transporter expression. Tumors glow because they burn glucose rapidly. The Warburg effect: cancer cells favor glycolysis even when oxygen is available.

lines: cancer is not what the tracer sees
PET reads a hunger for sugar

beats.new_visual_element: [GRAPHIC] two-column: what you think vs what PET reads

beats.narration_text: Glucose metabolism is not unique to cancer. Activated immune cells in an infection produce equally bright uptake. A healing surgical site glows for weeks. Brown adipose tissue — cold-activated fat in the neck and chest — mimics lymph node signal.

lines: cancer isn't the only thing that glows

card.copy: Glucose metabolism is not unique to cancer
card.sub: inflammation · healing wounds · brown adipose tissue

beats.new_visual_element: [CARD] section — three false-positive causes listed as sub

beats.narration_text: False negatives are equally real. Tumors with low glycolytic flux — well-differentiated thyroid cancers, some prostate cancers, mucin-secreting adenocarcinomas — may take up near-zero FDG despite substantial tumor burden. A dark scan is not an empty scan.

document.quote: A dark scan is not an empty scan.
document.attribution: — the FDG-negative lesion is metabolically quiet, not absent

beats.scene_description: large serif quote card; gold highlighter sweeps 'dark' as it is spoken
beats.new_visual_element: [QUOTE] a dark scan is not an empty scan

beats.narration_text: Every imaging signal is a proxy: it reports what tissue tends to do, not what the tissue is. This is why every clinical imaging report says 'consistent with' or 'suspicious for', never 'confirms'. Imaging suggests. Biopsy confirms.
beats.new_visual_element: [GRAPHIC] signal chain: imaging suggests, biopsy confirms

beats.narration_text: Illustrative case. A 58-year-old patient, breast cancer surgery three months prior. FDG-PET for recurrence surveillance. Three lymph nodes show high uptake in the chest. The team flags them for salvage radiation.
beats.scene_description: a printed case summary sheet or referral note on newsprint, annotated with three circled lymph node locations and 'high FDG uptake' notation — editorial, desaturated, slow pan across
beats.image_prompt: B09, a printed oncology referral note pinned to aged newsprint, handwritten annotations circling three lymph node locations labeled 'high FDG uptake', a small PET scan thumbnail in corner showing bright spots, desaturated editorial reproduction, flat print

beats.narration_text: Biopsy: all three are reactive lymph nodes. The patient had a mild upper-respiratory infection the week before the scan. No malignant cells in any of them. The scan reported correctly — elevated glucose metabolism in three nodes. The cause was wrong. Numbers are illustrative.

lines: a URI the week before the scan

beats.new_visual_element: [GRAPHIC] three nodes reveal as reactive — not malignant

beats.narration_text: The scanner performed correctly: it reported elevated glucose metabolism in three lymph nodes. The error was the interpretive assumption — that high metabolism equals cancer.

document.quote: The scanner was right. The assumption was wrong.
document.attribution: — high metabolism is not cancer; it is what cancer tends to do

beats.narration_text: FDG-PET measures glucose metabolism, not malignancy. Cancer is one of many conditions that raise it. Every imaging signal is a proxy: it reports what tissue tends to do, not what it is. Imaging suggests. Biopsy confirms.
